It's annoying to me how people always refer to WoW as if it were the first game in the genre. It might have been the first wildly popular one but it was not the first one people played. It took from Everquest and gave different visuals and arguably a more popular mechanic and underpinning and simplified the graphics into a cartoonish style. Back then, in both EQ and WoW, everything in it was new. EQ took the roleplaying to a bit of a classic level in that you had to actually type key phrases to NPCs and didn't compromise as much on the classical elements of role playing whereas WoW and everyone afterwards change the interface, interactions, mechanics, classes, etc ad nuseum to cater to what I call the "stupid or casual" people... they wanted to play this thing that looked cool but they couldn't handle the way you had to essentially stop action to think.

Take, for example, a guy I knew. He watched me play the shit out of Divinity Original Sin Enhanced. He only ever managed to watch me do combat, heard the music, and a top down isometric view and thought it was fast paced. Killing people, barrels that explode, run in and kill people, shoot an arrow and you get a cloud of status effects that killed enemies. He only ever saw the parts he was interested in (which wasn't the majority of the game). Since it has local multi-player with split screen, when he begged to play co-op with me, I said sure. It was only then that he realized that he hated the game. You HAD to read. You HAD to manage your inventory. You HAD to stop and think... quest lines, places in the world, swap gear and inventory for your upcoming challenges. You HAD to think through puzzles or go across the entire map to finish a quest only to trudge back to see what you had done. He lost interest in the first 45 minutes and never wanted to play again. He never got to the part where it becomes Inventory Management SimulatorTM.

Now, to be fair, the retard deliberately failed out of high school and is otherwise a perfect example of what not to be when you grow up. But his attitude towards gaming is the epitome of what the gaming industry needs to cater to. Not the niche where people want to have slower paced storytelling, reading, thinking, etc. They want the fast paced explosions and epic archetypes slapped into a pretty package.

So the modern MMO game needs to balance that. It is a victim of its own success where people flock to it and if the studio doesn't provide what the masses want, they take their money to people who will. When those numbers of people leave, it looks bad on sales, it generates an active lack of interest in the game and, with few exceptions, the game servers are shut down and studio closes. EQ, EQII, and numerous others have managed to avoid this by introducing non-required microtransactions and opening areas of the world where you previously needed to complete quests to access.

In other words, MMOs are required to appeal to the lowest common denominator. They need to pay attention to all these things that they don't have time to deal with the common problems (such as infinite grinding, lame quests, etc).

You need to think, plan, reserve your limited inventory as much as possible. Oh yeah, and steal :) but it's still a kind of single player MMO (RPG, if you want to be technical). With the growth of technology since the last Thief game was released, the kinds of games in that line which could be released now are mind-blowing if you really stop to think. But it is and will always be a niche market game because it doesn't cater to the lowest common denominator.
